goal.what: A newcomer decides from the README alone whether the product fits their work, and if it does, starts using it.

critical_success_factors.what: The reader knows whether the product fits their work.

necessary_conditions.what: Does the opening say what the product is, who it's for, and what it lets them achieve?
necessary_conditions.why: Most readers decide from the opening alone whether to read on, so it must let a newcomer tell within a few sentences whether the product is for them. Geoffrey Moore's positioning statement, from Crossing the Chasm, gives the decisions in order.

items.text: Decide the target: the people the product is for, named by the work they want done, narrowly enough that a reader outside the group can tell it isn't for them.
Decide their need: what they can't do well today, in their words.
Decide the category: a kind of thing the reader already knows, such as a command-line tool, which gives them something to compare it with.
Decide the key benefit: what they achieve with the product, taken from the objectives of the product vision, as an end they reach, not a feature.
Write the opening from these four, in words the reader already uses, and leave out feature names and internals.
Read only the opening, then put it away and explain the product as you would to a colleague. Shorten any part you forgot or got wrong.
Replace each vague or praising word in the opening with what the product does.
Read the opening as someone outside the target. If they couldn't tell that the product isn't for them, name the target and their work more precisely.

necessary_conditions.what: Does the README list what readers might expect the product to do but it doesn't?
necessary_conditions.why: A reader who needs something the product doesn't do should find out before they install it. The method is the non-goals of a design document, as in Malte Ubl's [Design Docs at Google](https://www.industrialempathy.com/posts/design-docs-at-google/): things that could reasonably be goals, listed to mark the edge of the scope where readers would otherwise guess.

items.text: Derive the expectations from the opening: its category and its key benefit lead a reader to expect certain things, such as undoing its changes from a tool that edits files.
For each thing the opening leads a reader to expect, ask whether the product does it, and whether its absence would change the reader's decision.
Ask the user about each expectation whose scope the product vision doesn't settle.
List only the expectations that the product doesn't meet and whose absence would change the reader's decision.
Where the product meets the need another way, say so in the same item.

necessary_conditions.what: Does the README say at the top where the product isn't ready for use yet?
necessary_conditions.why: A reader who builds on a product that isn't ready finds out only after their work depends on it. The method is the project states that [repostatus.org](https://www.repostatus.org) defines, such as Concept, Work in Progress, Active, and Unsupported.

items.text: Decide the product's state by the states that repostatus.org defines.
If the state is anything but Active, say it at the top, with what it means for the reader's work: what works now, and what they get if they install today.
Check that a newcomer can say, after the opening, whether they can rely on the product today.

necessary_conditions.what: Does the README name the license and link its full text?
necessary_conditions.why: Some readers rule a product in or out by its license alone, so they must find it at once and recognize it. The method is the identifiers of the [Software Package Data Exchange (SPDX) License List](https://spdx.org/licenses/), which readers and their tools recognize.

items.text: Take the license from the product's license file.
Name the license by its SPDX identifier.
Link the license's full text.
If the product includes work under other licenses, name each with its source.
Open the link and check that it leads to the license the README names.

necessary_conditions.what: Does the README answer each question in the order a reader comes to ask it?
necessary_conditions.why: Readers come with questions in a typical order, and leave when the next answer isn't where they look. The [inverted pyramid](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/inverted-pyramid/) puts first what every reader needs, for the same reason.

items.text: Decide the order by listing the readers and the question each has next. Every reader first asks what the product is and whether it's for them. A reader who has decided asks how to install it. A reader still deciding asks whether it really works, and how. A reader who has started asks where to learn more.
Order the sections so that each answer comes just when its question does, and each reader can stop once they have what they came for.
Read the README from the top as a newcomer, and after each section, write down the question you have next.
Remove what no reader needs at that point, or move it to a linked document.
Check that the next section answers that question. Move any section that answers a later one.

critical_success_factors.what: The reader learns what they get from the product in work like their own.

necessary_conditions.what: Does the walkthrough show a real run on typical work that delivers what the product vision's key results promise, in a form the reader can see?
necessary_conditions.why: A reader trusts a benefit they've seen happen more than one they only read about. Diátaxis calls this a [tutorial](https://diataxis.fr/tutorials/): one concrete task, carried through to a visible result.

items.text: Choose the use that most readers come for, taken from what readers ask for most and from the main use of the product vision's objectives.

Choose the task: one like the reader's own work, small enough to show from start to end, and real enough that the benefit shows in its result. If the result wouldn't show the benefit the opening promises, choose another task.
Decide the cut: show every exchange from what the reader gives to the result they keep, with the product's real output, and cut only what doesn't bear on the result.

Decide how each key result of the product vision shows in the run, since the key results say what the product promises. For how well, show the result in use as its users would use it. For how fast, show what the reader spent, such as the questions they answered.
Take each exchange from the record of a real run, in the form the reader meets it.
State the result first, so that the reader knows where the run goes.
Check that a newcomer can say, after reading, what the product would give them on their own work.

critical_success_factors.what: The reader understands why the product can give it, and trusts that it does.

necessary_conditions.what: Does How it works state first, in the reader's words, the one way that the product vision's concept puts first, and build the rest of its explanation from it?
necessary_conditions.why: A reader trusts a product they can explain to themselves, and they explain it from one idea, not from a list of parts. Barbara Minto's pyramid principle, in The Minto Pyramid Principle, puts one governing thought at the top and makes everything below support it.

items.text: Take the concept from the product vision.
Take the one way that the concept states first, which is what the product values most.
Say it in the reader's words, as what they see the product do in their work, in one sentence.
Build the figure and the answers of How it works below it, so that each part shows how it carries out that one way.
Check that a newcomer can say the one way back, and say how each answer follows from it.

necessary_conditions.what: Does How it works answer the problems and doubts that bring readers to the product, each by the part of the product that answers it and how that part follows from the one way?
necessary_conditions.why: A reader tries a product when the push of their problem and the pull of what the product gives them outweigh their doubts about it. Bob Moesta calls these the forces of progress, in Demand-Side Sales 101, from the theory of the jobs that customers hire a product for.

items.text: List the problems that the target reader would name in their work, and the doubts they would raise about the product, in their words, such as, for a backup tool, that their backups fail without warning, or whether it works with their network drive.
Keep only those whose answer would change whether the reader tries the product. A doubt that the walkthrough already settles needs nothing more.
For each one left, take the part of the product that answers it from the product vision's concept.
Where the concept has none, tell whether an idea that matters to the users is missing, or only the way to make it work.
Where an idea that matters to the users is missing, ask the user to add it to the product vision.
Where only the way to make it work is missing, record it in the design tree as a requirement that the architecture meets.
Put those parts together as one mechanism below the one way, and say for each part how it follows from that way.
Show the mechanism in one figure, with each problem and doubt beside the part that answers it, and what the reader gets from that part.
Label each part in the reader's words.
Where a part has a name of the product's own, explain the part in a few words.
Check that a newcomer can say back how the product gives them what it promises, and why they can trust that it does.

critical_success_factors.what: The reader installs the product and starts using it without help.

necessary_conditions.what: Can a reader with nothing set up install the product by the README alone, and see that it works?
necessary_conditions.why: A reader who can't install the product never gets to use it, and the author's own setup hides what a newcomer lacks. [Standard Readme](https://github.com/RichardLitt/standard-readme) holds these in its Install section.

items.text: Take each requirement and each install command from the product's manifest and code, never from memory.
Starting from a machine with nothing on it, list everything the product needs.
For each requirement, choose a command whose output shows that the reader has it.
Write each install step as a command the reader can copy.
End the steps with a sign the reader can see that the product works.

On a machine or sandbox with nothing the product needs, follow the steps exactly as written. If a step fails or needs something the README doesn't mention, a requirement is missing: add it and start again.

necessary_conditions.what: Does the README link where to go for fuller use and for help?
necessary_conditions.why: The README stays short only if each later need has its own place to go. Each need has its own kind of page, which [Diátaxis](https://diataxis.fr) sorts into tutorials, how-to guides, reference, and explanation.

items.text: List what a reader needs after they start, such as fuller use, reference, help, and the changes in each version.
Give one link for each need, with whom it's for.
Open each link, and check that it opens the page it names.
